newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn embarks on revamp to ready its mkts for euro.
newsitem.headline: Bonn embarks on revamp to ready its mkts for euro.

text.p: Germany's finance ministry on Tuesday unveiled a critical paper drawn up with banks, insurers, issuers and the stock exchange to identify weaknesses in its financial centre amid growing international competition.

Warning that the 1999 launch of Europe's single currency, the euro, and the trend to globalisation of markets meant that action had to be taken now, a senior finance ministry official laid out a catalogue of action points for Germany.

Juergen Stark, state secretary to Bonn's finance ministry, told a news conference: "There is no doubt that further work is needed to adjust individual sectors of the financial centre to the needs of international financial markets."

Germany needed a better investment banking infrastructure, more liberalisation of its bourse and labour laws, a more open policy on financial innovation to ensure speedier introduction on new instruments and a greater role for its stock exchange in offering funding to companies, Stark said.

Investment in the equities market needed to be encouraged while German Finance Minister Theo Waigel had already agreed to plans to strengthen the capital market by converting existing government debt to euros on the currency's launch in 1999, Stark said.

Germany has already made significant efforts, including legislation to criminalise insider trading and enforce market transparency, to boost the standing of its "Finanzplatz", or financial centre, after years of being regarded as being short on investor protection and adequate codes for market behaviour.
The latest package of financial market improvements will be discussed in the Bonn cabinet next week.
But it has not yet managed to shake off repeated criticism that the German market is slow to adapt to changing conditions.

"The hope is that soon no one will be able to say 'German markets are slow to catch on but quick to catch up', but rather that they are 'Quick to catch on and to catch up'," the paper said in its concluding paragraph.
Yet Stark warned that the plan was not to offer a "Big Bang" solution, such as that proposed for Japanese markets, but rather a gradual improvement of the operating environment.
He also made clear that Germany did not intend simply to adopt wholesale the practices and regulations followed in the world's leading financial market, the United States.

"If we are taking further steps here to promote the financial centre, that is not a question of giving up the principle of long-termism and adopting pure short-termism. We do not want this and cannot do it. It would not be in line with our culture," he said.
The German economy still rests heavily on the principles of consensus and burden-sharing adopted as the country rebuilt itself after the destruction of World War Two.

Its corporate structure is characterised by a backbone of small firms, many of which are still family held, and an intricate network of cross-shareholdings within industry which spills over into the banking sector.
The long-term nature of the bulk of these shareholdings has led Germany to develop a culture of "stakeholder value", rather than the more familiar "shareholder value" usual in the U.S.
"Ideally we would combine the best of both of these," Stark said. "Although the U.S. system has a more short-term approach it also has a positive market and competitive orientation."

Now that the main areas of weakness had been pinpointed in the paper, concrete proposals for change would have to come from parties involved in the working group which drew up the draft -- banks, insurers, the bourse, market participants, theoreticians and the government itself -- Stark said.
The working group -- called Forum Finanzplatz -- would also work closely with the recently-formed lobby group Aktionskreis Finanzplatz e.V., he added.

Germany's main financial centre, Frankfurt, is currently the top financial centre in continental Europe. On a global scale, Germany sees Frankfurt as the fourth largest centre after New York, London and Tokyo.
The German bourse Deutsche Boerse AG in April announced plans of its own to try to expand its activities and draw more privately-held money into equities.
